sections.title: The compass and its surroundings
paragraphs: A magnetic compass can show a direction without a distant landmark. Its needle can turn freely in response to the magnetic field at its location. In many ordinary settings, the Earth's field has a strong enough horizontal component to guide the needle. That makes the compass useful in fog or in a place where the horizon cannot be seen. However, the device responds to the field that is actually present around it. It has no way to identify which part of that field comes from the Earth. A reading taken near a source of interference can therefore look stable while indicating a direction different from the one a traveller intended to measure.

To obtain a reading, the needle must be able to rotate without rubbing against the case. Holding the compass level helps the needle move freely in a model designed to be used that way. The user can then wait for the movement to settle before reading the scale. Turning the case quickly during this process can make the reading harder to interpret, because the needle is still responding while the marks beneath it are being moved. A clear routine separates holding the instrument, waiting and reading. It also makes it easier to compare two results, since both can be taken with the needle and case in a similar state.

Magnetic north is not necessarily the direction to the geographic North Pole. The angle between the magnetic direction and geographic north is called declination. The angle varies with location and can also change over time. A map that provides a value for a particular place may state the date to which the value applies. Before using a compass reading with a map, a navigator should check how the two references are related. An error in the sign of the adjustment can send the traveller farther from the desired direction instead of correcting the reading. It is useful to understand the reference before applying a remembered rule.

A nearby magnet can produce an obvious change. Less obvious sources include some metal objects that can affect the field close to the compass. A user taking a reading beside a vehicle may obtain a different result after stepping away from it. Small personal items can also matter if they are held very close to the instrument. One practical check is to take several readings from nearby positions while keeping the distant landmark or intended direction fixed. If the readings change sharply when the instrument moves a short distance, that variation suggests checking the surroundings rather than averaging the values as if they were equivalent.

The compass scale can still be misread when the magnetic conditions are satisfactory. The end of the needle used for the reading must be identified, and the marks on the scale have to be read from the intended side. A traveller who reverses the selected end can obtain a direction pointing back along the same line. The mistake is sometimes easier to notice when a map or a visible feature provides an independent check. If the road expected on one side appears on the other, it is worth checking the whole procedure. Altering the route immediately without checking could hide the source of the error.

A direction is often easier to follow by selecting a visible point on the line and walking to it. This avoids the need to watch the needle with every step. Near an obstacle, a traveller may have to move away from the line and then return to it. Keeping track of the side on which the obstacle was passed helps with the return. In poor visibility, a closer point may be needed because a distant one cannot be seen reliably. The compass gives a direction, while the choice of points and the handling of obstacles belong to the navigation plan. Both contribute to whether the traveller reaches the intended place.

The value of a compass increases when its reading can be compared with other information. A traveller can check whether a slope falls in the direction expected from the map or whether a marked crossing lies at the expected angle. A disagreement has several possible causes, including a mistaken location, a reading error or interference near the needle. It should be investigated before it is treated as proof that one source is wrong. The most useful record says where the reading was taken and how it was checked. That context helps someone repeat the observation or explain why a later reading differs.

sections.title: How a paper filter separates a mixture
paragraphs: A paper filter holds back some parts of a mixture while allowing others to pass. In a simple arrangement, the paper is supported in a funnel and the liquid is poured into it. Small spaces between fibres provide routes through the paper. Particles that cannot pass through those routes can remain on the surface or within the paper. The liquid that emerges is called the filtrate. A clear filtrate can show that many visible particles have been removed. It cannot by itself show that all the substances that were present have been removed, because substances dissolved in the liquid can travel through with it.

The path of a particle through a filter is rarely a perfectly straight passage. Fibres overlap, and the available openings differ in size. A particle may turn, meet a narrow point or attach to the surface of a fibre. Its shape can therefore matter as well as its largest width. A long narrow particle may fit through an opening in one orientation but not in another. A description of a filter by one nominal size is useful as a guide, but the actual mixture can behave more gradually than a division into particles that always pass and particles that always stop. Testing with the intended mixture gives better evidence.

A filter changes as material collects on it. The retained particles can form a layer that offers additional resistance to the flow. That layer may hold back smaller particles than the paper initially did. At the same time, the liquid can pass more slowly. An observer who compares only the first and last portions of the liquid may therefore see differences even if the mixture entering the filter was the same. It is useful to record when each sample was collected and whether the filter had already been used. The state of the filter is part of the conditions under which its performance was observed.

The way the paper is fitted can be as important as the paper itself. If a gap remains at the edge, some liquid may travel around the paper instead of passing through it. A filter with fine openings is of little help to the part of the mixture taking that shorter path. Pouring too quickly can also lift the edge or send liquid over it. Checking the fit before a test helps distinguish poor separation caused by the material from poor separation caused by the arrangement. A comparison between two papers should keep the fitting and pouring method sufficiently similar for the difference between them to mean something.

Some tasks require a choice between speed and separation. A paper that holds back smaller particles can take longer to pass the same volume. A coarse first filter can sometimes remove large material before a finer stage. That can reduce the load placed on the fine paper and make the overall process more practical. It also adds a stage at which some liquid may be lost. The writer favours starting with a clear statement of what must be removed and what must be recovered. A filter that gives the clearest liquid may be a poor choice if the task also requires a particular volume in a limited time.

There are also situations in which the retained material, rather than the liquid, is the useful part. Recovering it may require a way to remove it from the paper without adding fibres or losing a substantial amount. A mixture that includes both useful and unwanted particles can require another separation step. In that case, a successful first filtration is one that prepares the mixture for that next step. Judging the filter by the clarity of the liquid alone would overlook the actual purpose. A useful report should say whether the performance being assessed is recovery of the solid, clarity of the liquid or a combination of the two.

A basic comparison can use the same starting volume, the same type of mixture and a recorded period of filtration. The investigator can then examine both how much liquid was collected and what remained in it. If the aim is to remove a dissolved substance, paper filtration may be the wrong process to test. That conclusion is itself useful. It prevents a clear-looking sample from being interpreted as proof of a chemical change. By matching the separation method to the form in which the unwanted material occurs, the investigator can make the trial answer the intended question. The visible result is one observation within that account.

sections.title: How a label changes the way an exhibit is read
paragraphs: A museum label is short enough to seem secondary to the object it describes. Yet the label often directs attention to details that a visitor would otherwise overlook. It can identify a material, suggest where an object was held or give a reason to examine a particular mark. Different descriptions can therefore lead visitors to look at different parts of the same object. A label cannot present every relevant fact at once. The writer regards the selection of a first detail as a decision about what kind of encounter the visitor will have, rather than simply a matter of reducing the length of a longer description.

One difficulty is that the first word used to classify an object may settle an open question too early. Calling a worn wooden piece a handle tells a reader to imagine it attached to another object. If its use is uncertain, that word can present an interpretation as if it were an observation. A description can instead say that the piece has a smooth area where a hand could have held it. This gives visitors something they can inspect while leaving the proposed use open to question. A label can mention the interpretation as a possibility and still distinguish it from the visible features on which the interpretation rests.

The sequence in which evidence is presented matters as well. A visitor who reads a conclusion first may then notice mainly the details that support it. Presenting a question before the conclusion can invite a different kind of looking. For instance, a label could ask the visitor to compare two worn edges before explaining what the comparison might suggest about use. This approach works best when the relevant details can actually be seen. If they are hidden by the way an object is displayed, the label may need an image or another form of explanation. A question should give the visitor a usable task rather than simply delaying the answer.

Labels can also make a collection appear more complete than it is. A series of objects displayed in date order can suggest an unbroken sequence even when the objects come from a few places with unusually good preservation. The writer favours making important gaps explicit. A short sentence can say that a period is poorly represented because objects made from a certain material seldom survive. That information changes what the sequence can be used to infer. It does not undermine the objects that are present. Instead, it helps a visitor distinguish the history of a practice from the history of what happened to survive in the collection.

Space and time place real limits on what can be read. A visitor standing in a busy room may read only a heading and the first few lines. Important qualifications buried at the end can therefore fail to influence the interpretation formed at the start. One response is to place the uncertainty close to the claim it qualifies. Additional detail can be available separately for visitors who want to continue. The writer does not require every visitor to read the same amount. The goal is for the shorter version to remain accurate on its own, while the longer one makes the reasons for the interpretation easier to examine.

The language of a label should also match what it asks the visitor to do. Technical terms are useful where they name a distinction that ordinary words would blur. An unfamiliar term with no explanation can prevent the visitor from noticing the distinction at all. A definition is especially helpful when it can point to an example on the object. The term then becomes a tool for looking rather than an isolated fact to remember. A label can use precise language and remain accessible if it gives the reader a way to connect each important word to something that can be observed or understood in that setting.

A strong label can therefore be evaluated by following the visitor’s reasoning. Which feature is noticed first? What claim does the label make about it, and what evidence is offered for the claim? Where does it ask the visitor to keep a possibility open? Such questions can reveal a problem that counting words or checking individual facts would miss. A label can be factually accurate in every sentence yet lead readers towards an inference that the evidence does not support. The better test is whether the label helps a visitor see the object and understand which conclusions can reasonably be drawn from it.
